title: A peer self-harm death can spread risk through a youth social network while care and offending responses diverge
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35603, linked South Carolina administrative data on peer self-harm deaths and surviving students
geography: South Carolina students and linked administrative health, education, and criminal-justice records

observations.period: Student peer self-harm deaths and matched post-exposure outcomes in the study's South Carolina administrative panel

denominator.unit: Students and peer-death exposure events in linked South Carolina administrative data; exact public abstract denominator not disclosed

exposure_prevalence.value: by age 17, about one-quarter of U.S. students have experienced a peer suicide
exposure_prevalence.unit: reported national context, not the South Carolina study denominator

self_harm_diagnosis.value: exposure to a peer's self-harm death increased the probability of a self-harm diagnosis by nearly 50%

mental_health_visits.value: both the incidence and frequency of mental-health visits increased after exposure

heterogeneous_response.value: care-use and criminal-behavior effects were concentrated among white boys; students without a prior diagnosis increased felony offending rather than care-seeking

comparison_deaths.value: assault and transportation deaths produced no comparable rise in self-harm

later_recovery.value: not observed in the public abstract
later_recovery.unit: missing school continuity, family support, treatment completion, later self-harm, safety, and adult outcomes

observations.method: Linked South Carolina administrative data and matched difference-in-differences comparing students exposed to a peer's self-harm death with matched students; assault and transportation deaths serve as comparison events.
observations.uncertainty: The public abstract does not disclose exact sample counts, exposure timing details, all subgroup estimates, or the full follow-up horizon. The study is South Carolina-specific and administrative diagnoses and visits do not capture all distress, support, or informal care.
observations.subgroup: Surviving students, with reported heterogeneity by race/sex subgroup and prior mental-health diagnosis; school, family, neighborhood, friendship, and treatment-level pathways are not fully linked in the abstract.
observations.counterinterpretation: Increased diagnoses and care visits can reflect greater need, better detection, or more help-seeking. The comparison-death pattern is consistent with contagion but does not isolate every social, family, school, media, or community mechanism.

related_sources.claim: The 988 capacity study supplies a contrasting crisis-system operations layer without a detectable short-run population mortality effect.

boundary: This record measures peer-death exposure and short-run administrative self-harm, mental-health-visit, and criminal-behavior responses in South Carolina. It does not establish a national rate, individual contagion mechanism, completed suicide effect, school or family causal pathway, or later recovery outcome.
